projects.title: 01 - Full Overview over Unreal Engine 5
projects.summary: Begin your game development journey. Master the Unreal Engine 5 interface, configure projects, and learn the essential tools needed for the 3D transition ahead.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Embark on your game development journey with my comprehensive overview of Unreal Engine 5. This tutorial serves as your ultimate foundation, guiding you through the Epic Games Launcher, optimal project setups, and a detailed tour of the Unreal Engine editor interface to kickstart your creative vision.

### 1. Navigating the Epic Games Launcher
Your Gateway to State-of-the-Art Game Development
- Explore the Unreal Engine tab, discovering essential community resources, marketplace assets, and powerful sample projects like Lyra and the City Sample.
- Learn how to manage your project library, download different engine versions, and leverage the monthly free assets to build up your development vault.

### 2. Setting Up Your First Project
C++ vs. Blueprints and Performance Presets
- Dive into the Unreal Engine Project Browser to choose the right template for your game, cinematic, or architectural project.
- Understand the crucial differences between Blueprint and C++ project setups, and learn how to configure scalability and screen percentage settings to ensure smooth performance on your PC.

### 3. Mastering the Editor Interface
A Tour of the Workspace
- Get comfortable with the core editor menus, understanding the relationship between the Viewport, Outliner, and the Content Drawer.
- Learn essential navigation controls for moving the camera seamlessly, utilizing grid snapping, and organizing your assets effectively for rapid development.

### 4. Exploring Advanced Engine Modes
Landscape, Foliage, and Fracturing
- Discover how to build sprawling open worlds using the built-in Landscape sculpting and Foliage painting tools.
- Uncover unique built-in features like the Chaos destruction system using the Fracture tool, and the Modelling mode for manipulating assets directly within the engine.

### 5. Viewport Rendering and Nanite Visualization
Optimizing What You See
- Explore advanced viewport options, from altering local and world coordinate systems to utilizing cinematic controls.
- Dive into Unreal Engine's unique Nanite rendering by activating visualization modes to debug your geometry, Lumen lighting, and overall scene optimization.

### 6. Conclusion: Ready to Build in UE5?
Laying the Groundwork for Your Next Game
- Congratulations on completing your first Unreal Engine 5 overview! You are now equipped with a solid understanding of the UI and core operational modes.
- Stay tuned for upcoming lessons in this series where we will dive deeper into Blueprints, C++ programming, and bringing your own open worlds to life.

projects.title: 02 - Stockfish Integration
projects.summary: Build the brain of your chess game. Integrate the Stockfish AI using pure C++ to calculate optimal moves and handle complex rules without writing them from scratch.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Welcome to the first coding lecture of our 3D Chess project in Unreal Engine. To get the basics right, we are starting with a console program and integrating the Stockfish application in the background. This approach allows us to see how standard C++ differs from Unreal C++ and helps us outsource the complex chess rules, legal moves, and AI calculations directly to Stockfish.

### 1. Project Architecture and CMake
Understanding the File Structure
We start by looking at the provided project folder containing the Stockfish executables for Windows, Mac, and Linux. You will learn why using local executables is safer than relying on web APIs that can break over time. We will also cover CMake lists, which ensure our C++ code compiles seamlessly across different operating systems.

### 2. Compiling in Visual Studio
Setting Up the Development Environment
Learn how to open the project in Visual Studio, which is the exact development environment Unreal Engine uses for compilation. We will configure the executable paths, making sure to use double backslashes for Windows, and run our very first CMake build to see the base console program in action.

### 3. The Stockfish C++ Implementation
Managing the Engine Instance
Dive into the Stockfish C++ file to understand how we communicate with the engine. We will explore the Singleton pattern, which prevents the program from opening hundreds of stockfish instances and crashing your GPU. You will also learn how to create a pipeline to send commands and read vector-based string arrays as outputs.

### 4. Stockfish API and UCI Commands
Communicating with the "AI"
We take a look at the official Stockfish documentation and test commands directly in the executable. You will learn the core Universal Chess Interface (UCI) commands, such as checking if the engine is ready, setting thread values, and asking the "AI" to calculate the best possible moves based on specific depths and skill levels.

### 5. Decoding the FEN Notation
Translating the Board State
Discover the importance of Forsyth-Edwards Notation (FEN). This string format records the entire board state, including piece placement, active color, castling rights, and move counts. You will learn how our C++ code parses the Stockfish response to extract FEN strings, best moves, and legal moves, translating them into an easy-to-read console output.

### 6. Conclusion: Preparing for the Next Steps
Laying the "AI" Foundation
By the end of this lesson, you have successfully set up the AI handler for our chess game. We have covered the complex interaction with Stockfish so that we never have to worry about coding chess rules from scratch. Next time, we will write the FEN parser and build out the actual console chess interaction.

projects.title: 03 - FEN-Extraction
projects.summary: Translate AI logic into readable data. Write a custom C++ parser to decode FEN strings, extracting piece positions and special rules for the game board.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Welcome back to the third lecture of our Unreal Engine chess project series! In this tutorial, we dive deep into the Forsyth-Edwards Notation (FEN) and focus primarily on how to extract and parse FEN strings using C++. By thoroughly understanding FEN structures, you will be able to flawlessly convert board states, rules, and game logic into a format that both Stockfish and our console program can understand.

### 1. Understanding the FEN String Structure
Decoding the Board State
- Get a comprehensive breakdown of what makes up a FEN string, including board representation, turn color, castling rights, En Passant targets, half-move clocks, and full-move numbers.
- Learn how the alphanumeric characters correspond to specific chess pieces (e.g., P for Pawn, R for Rook) and how uppercase versus lowercase determines the piece's color.
- Understand how numeric values in the string represent empty squares, and how slashes divide the rows of the chessboard.

### 2. Implementing the Parse FEN Function
Building the Parser in C++
- Discover how to split the FEN string into its six core components utilizing standard C++ string streams and spaces as delimiters.
- Implement error handling to default back to a standard starting FEN string in case of corrupted or invalid inputs.
- Learn the technique of utilizing dynamic std::vector<std::string> containers over standard arrays to securely parse an unlimited stream of data without memory overflow concerns.

### 3. Constructing the Board Representation
Iterating Through the Rows
- Walk through the process of slicing the board state string by its row-defining slashes.
- Convert character digits back to mathematical integers to correctly push empty squares (represented by dots .) to our board state vector.
- Evaluate the exact index conditions to successfully assign White and Black turns based on the parsed characters.

### 4. Managing Complex Rules: Castling and En Passant
Setting the Rules of Engagement
- Parse the FEN string to determine specific castling availabilities for both the King and Queen sides.
- Unpack the complex logic and conditional formatting required to recognize an En Passant square target.
- Set up parsing variables to convert half-move and full-move clocks from strings to integers, enabling automatic draw offers based on the 100-move rule.

### 5. Handling Special Move Notations for 3D Environments
Refining Outputs for Unreal Engine
- Understand why basic Stockfish move outputs (like A7B8Q) are insufficient for a 3D physical environment where pieces must visibly move, lift, and collide.
- Learn how to program custom special rule signatures into the engine's response string.
- Detect promotions, alter strings to inject arrows for piece swaps, and write customized checks for negative moves and squares under attack to guarantee fluid 3D castling and En Passant animations.

### 6. Conclusion: Ready for the Console
Wrapping up the Logic
- Congratulations on completing the algorithmic heavy lifting of FEN extraction! You now have a working parser capable of decoding and augmenting any FEN string.
- In our next lecture, we will wrap up this logic by injecting it directly into our finalized console chess program.

projects.title: 04 - Console-Chess
projects.summary: Complete the foundational C++ phase. Build the core game loop and manage player turns in a text-based console, finalizing the logic before jumping into 3D.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Welcome to the fourth and final lecture of the plain C++ section! In this lesson, we wrap up our foundational work by implementing an interactive console game where we can finally play chess against the Stockfish AI or another player locally. This fully functional text-based game serves as the perfect stepping stone before we transition into Unreal Engine 5 to reconstruct this exact logic in a 3D environment.

### 1. The Standard Game Loop
Structuring Game Logic
Learn the core difference between internal game loops and standard game loops that require user input. We dissect the architecture of our chess program, exploring how to structure the initialization phase (getting player names and difficulties) before entering a continuous while-true loop that processes moves, updates the board state, and checks for win conditions.

### 2. Structs, Enums, and Maps in C++
Managing Player Details
Discover how to keep track of game data cleanly using C++ data structures. We use Enums to intuitively assign "White" and "Black" instead of simple integers, and we create Structs to bundle player names with a boolean that flags whether the player is a human or an AI. Finally, we map these details together so the game always knows whose turn it is and how to address them.

### 3. Building the Initialization Flow
Validating User Inputs
Walk through the code that asks players to set up the game. You will learn how to capture inputs using std::getline and write secure while(true) loops to strictly enforce valid answers (like demanding a "yes" or "no", or ensuring the AI skill level is exactly an integer between 0 and 20).

### 4. Managing Turns and AI Responses
Alternating Game States
Understand the mathematical logic behind alternating turns using the Modulo operator, effortlessly switching the active player state from White (0) to Black (1) and back. We also explore the print functions that display the Stockfish response - including the FEN string, the ASCII board representation, and the list of legal moves - directly into the console.

### 5. Processing Moves and Win Conditions
Connecting the Player to the Engine
Dive into the most crucial part of the loop: checking the win state and processing player moves. Learn how to write checks that announce a Checkmate or a Draw, and how to scrub user inputs of excess spaces. You will see how we handle special rules seamlessly by removing the custom tags (like arrows and pipes for castling and promotions) so Stockfish can accurately read the raw command.

### 6. Conclusion: Transitioning to Unreal Engine
Ready for 3D
Congratulations on completing the C++ console chess program! You now have a working, robust chess engine capable of AI vs AI, Player vs Player, and Player vs AI matches at varying difficulty levels. In the next lectures, we will leave the console behind and start bringing this powerful logic to life in a visually stunning 3D environment using Unreal Engine 5.

projects.title: 05 - Chess-Pattern
projects.summary: Step into the 3D world of Unreal Engine 5. Connect your C++ code with visual Blueprints to procedurally generate and optimize the physical chessboard grid.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Welcome to the fifth lecture and the official transition from plain C++ to a full 3D environment in Unreal Engine 5! Today, we dive into how Unreal Engine utilizes both standard C++ code and Blueprints to build our interactive 3D chess game. We will start by thoroughly exploring the project structure and generating our first procedural elements, specifically constructing the physical chessboard pattern algorithmically.

### 1. Setting up Unreal Engine and Visual Studio
Connecting Your Development Environments
Learn how to safely generate and open your Unreal Engine project files inside Visual Studio for real-time editing. We also cover how to use Unreal's built-in Live Coding feature if you prefer modifying files without Visual Studio integration.

### 2. Optimizing Unreal Engine Performance
Achieving Stable Framerates on Any Machine
Unreal Engine can be heavy on resources, so this section focuses on critical performance optimization. Learn how to toggle Screen Percentage overrides, drop the Engine Scalability settings, and adjust Material Quality levels so your 3D workspace runs smoothly, even on lower-end hardware.

### 3. Navigating the Content Drawer
A Tour of Your 3D Assets
Take a guided tour through the project's Content Drawer. We dissect the differences between Static Meshes, Skeletal Meshes, Materials, and Textures. You will discover exactly where your core game logic is stored, from the Game Mode to interactive assets like the dartboard and the blank chessboard map.

### 4. Understanding Unreal Blueprints
Visual Scripting for Designers and Programmers
Discover the power of Unreal Engine Blueprints, a node-based visual programming language. We break down the Event Graph, the Viewport, and the Construction Script, explaining how visual scripting works seamlessly alongside your C++ parent classes to create a shared programming experience.

### 5. C++ Conversion and Algorithmic Instancing
Translating Data and Procedural Generation
Before standard C++ logic can work in Unreal, we translate standard data types like strings and vectors into Unreal's proprietary engine types. We then write the algorithmic logic to calculate 3D vector coordinates, efficiently spawning the alternating black and white tiles dynamically via the construction script.

### 6. Conclusion: Preparing for the Chess Pieces
A Solid Foundation
Congratulations! You have successfully spawned a fully interactive 3D chessboard using procedural C++ logic inside Unreal Engine 5. You now understand how to navigate the engine, tweak your performance, and use Blueprints alongside C++. Next time, we will bring this board to life by procedurally spawning all of the chess pieces dynamically.

projects.title: 06 - ChessPiece-Spawning
projects.summary: Populate your newly built 3D board. Use custom Blueprint macros and C++ to read the FEN string data and dynamically spawn the correct chess pieces in real-time.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Welcome to the sixth lecture of our Unreal Engine 5 chess project! In this tutorial, we are taking our procedural chessboard to the next level by automatically populating it with 3D chess pieces. By the end of this lesson, you will learn how to read FEN strings in C++ to determine piece positions and how to use Blueprint macros with custom loops to spawn these pieces dynamically onto the board.

### 1. Recap of Relevant Chess Components
Understanding the Core Blueprints
Before diving into the code, we review the three main components of our chess logic. The ChessBoard handles all the overarching operations and stores the board state. The ChessTile manages its own localized logic, such as highlighting its mesh for legal moves. Finally, the ChessPiece acts as the parent class for all pieces, containing the foundational logic for physical movement, jumping, and castling.

### 2. C++ Logic for Spawning Pieces
Bridging the FEN String to 3D Space
We transition into Visual Studio to review the C++ function responsible for spawning pieces onto the board. You will learn how the code extracts individual characters from the current FEN string and matches them against a predefined map of chess piece classes. This ensures that the engine knows exactly whether to instantiate a King, Queen, Pawn, or any other piece based strictly on text data.

### 3. Setting Piece Colors and Transforms
Configuring Materials and Locations
Once the engine knows which piece to spawn, it needs to determine its team color and exact physical location. We examine how the C++ code uses the capitalization of the FEN character to dynamically apply either the light or dark material to the mesh. We also calculate the 3D transform by grabbing the respective tile's location and applying an offset so the piece sits perfectly on top of the board without clipping.

### 4. Initializing the Game Mode
Triggering the Spawn Event
With the C++ logic covered, we head back into the Unreal Engine Blueprint editor. We look at the Game Mode and ChessBoard event graphs to hook up our new spawning mechanics. You will learn how the game initialization sequence parses the FEN string at the beginning of the match, clears any existing pieces, and passes the fresh data directly into our piece-spawning execution flow.

### 5. Building the Spawn Macro
Executing the Spawning Sequence
To keep our Event Graph clean and organized, we encapsulate the complex spawning logic inside a dedicated Blueprint macro. We walk through how this macro iterates over the extracted board state array, verifies if a specific tile requires a piece, and calls our C++ spawning function for every valid character, effectively rebuilding the entire physical board state in the 3D environment.

### 6. Creating a Custom ForEach Loop and Conclusion
Adding Polish with Sequential Delays
Standard Blueprint loops execute instantaneously, which can cause pieces to appear abruptly in a single frame. To improve the visual polish, we build a custom loop macro from scratch that supports execution delays. This allows us to pop the chess pieces onto the board sequentially for a much smoother effect. Congratulations on successfully spawning your chess pieces! In the next lesson, we will start making these pieces fully interactive.

projects.title: 06.5 - Special: Full Chess-Party Explanation
projects.summary: Pause to review the game architecture. Deepen your understanding of how C++ bridges with Blueprints and master memory optimization before coding player inputs.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Welcome to this special add-on lecture for the Unreal Engine 5 chess project! This bonus video serves as a comprehensive deep dive aimed at raising your understanding of the underlying code concepts. Because the project spans multiple systems, from standard C++ and Stockfish to Unreal Blueprints, this full walkthrough ties everything together, ensuring you have a rock-solid grasp of the entire architecture before moving on to player inputs.

### 1. Project Architecture Overview
Connecting the Chess Components
We begin with a holistic overview of the entire Chess-Party project file structure. You will review how the plain C++ scripts containing the Stockfish engine and FEN parsing logic successfully interface with Unreal Engine actor classes. Understanding this relationship is crucial for debugging and expanding your game later.

### 2. Game Mode and Initialization Flow
Tracing the Execution Path
Step into the core authority of our chess match, the Game Mode. This section provides a detailed trace of the execution flow the moment the game starts. We break down how the engine reads the initial variables, triggers the board generation, and handles the sequential spawning of all chess pieces.

### 3. The C++ and Blueprint Bridge
Understanding Macros and Node Logic
One of the most complex concepts is how C++ shares data with visual Blueprints. We dissect the specific macros, UProperties, and Blueprint Callable functions used in the project. You will see exactly why certain logic is kept in code for performance, while visual rendering and execution flow are handed off to node-based Blueprints.

### 4. Advanced FEN String Mechanics
Managing the Board State
A thorough review of the FEN extraction algorithms inside the engine. We explore the hidden complexities of managing turn states, handling string updates dynamically, and properly resetting the array of legal moves. This includes a closer look at how special moves like Castling and En Passant dictate changes in the physical board state.

### 5. Optimization and Memory Management
Demystifying Instanced Spawning
We take a closer look under the hood at the Hierarchical Instanced Static Mesh components used for our chessboard. This section explains the importance of instancing versus spawning individual actors, showing you how the project maintains optimal memory efficiency and high framerates despite managing dozens of tiles and interactive pieces.

### 6. Conclusion: Consolidating Your Knowledge
Ready for Interactive Gameplay
Congratulations on completing this comprehensive project review! By revisiting the core mechanics from a top-down perspective, you have reinforced your understanding of how Unreal Engine processes complex AI logic and transforms it into 3D visualizations. Next time, we will jump back into the main course to implement player inputs and interactive move selection.

projects.title: 07 - Move-Selection
projects.summary: Make your 3D game interactive using pure Blueprints. Build a visual state machine to handle mouse clicks, highlight valid tiles, and select legal moves.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Welcome to the seventh lecture of our Unreal Engine 5 chess project! This is our first lecture relying entirely on visual Blueprints without writing any new C++ code. Today, we focus on building the interactive move selection, allowing players to navigate the board and select valid chess moves using simple mouse clicks, moving away from text-based console inputs.

### 1. Recap of Unreal Engine Progress
Reviewing the Chessboard and Game Mode
We begin with a quick review of the current project state, ensuring that your procedural chessboard is generating properly and pieces are spawning via the FEN string logic built in previous lectures. We also review the construction script to ensure our hierarchical instanced static meshes are set up correctly before adding interaction.

### 2. Game Mode Initialization and FEN Strings
Handling Board States
We explore the Game Mode Blueprint to understand how the initial board state is loaded and how turns are managed. You will see how the engine communicates with Stockfish to parse the FEN string, determine whose turn it is, and evaluate end-game states like Checkmate or a Draw.

### 3. The Game State and AI Logic
Processing Stockfish Responses
We dive into the Game State to examine how AI moves are processed and translated into physical teleportations on the board. We cover how the AI's best move is extracted, mapped to the correct start and target tiles, and how special move strings (like castling or en passant) are matched against our legal moves array.

### 4. Implementing a Blueprint State Machine
Controlling Tile Interactions
To manage player inputs smoothly, we build a lightweight State Machine inside the Chess Tile Blueprint. You will learn how to assign varying states to individual tiles, such as inactive, highlighted, selected, under attack, and currently moving. This ensures that visual highlights and click events only trigger when the game logic allows it.

### 5. Building the Click Logic
Visual Scripting for Move Selection
We transition to live coding with Blueprints to build the actual mouse-click logic. You will learn how to map the Left Mouse Button to state changes, utilize custom macros to verify the tile's current state, and check if the user's selected target tile is actually contained within Stockfish's list of valid legal moves.

### 6. Refining the User Experience
Adding Right-Click Reversals
A crucial part of game design is usability. If a player clicks the wrong piece, they shouldn't be soft-locked. We finalize our Blueprint logic by mapping the Right Mouse Button to act as a cancel action. This allows players to smoothly revert a tile's state from under attack back to selected, or completely clear the selection and start over.

projects.title: 08 - AI-Movement
projects.summary: Polish the final chess experience. Replace instant teleports with smooth AI pathfinding, custom jump animations, and stunning Niagara particle effects for captures.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Welcome to the eighth and final lecture of the Chess-Party project! In this lesson, we replace the basic teleportation logic with smooth, AI-driven movement for our 3D chess pieces. We will also implement particle effects using Niagara, handle complex special moves like En Passant and Pawn Promotion visually, and squash any bugs with rigorous testing, culminating in a fully interactive, polished 3D chess game.

### 1. Transitioning to AI Movement
Replacing Teleportation with AI Nodes
We start by swapping out the basic set actor location logic in our Blueprint with the powerful "AI Move To" node. You will learn how to configure the agent pawn, assign target destinations, and utilize navigation meshes (NavMesh) within the level so pieces can intelligently navigate to their correct tiles without clipping through walls or obstacles.

### 2. Handling Navigation Failures
Building Failsafes with Retriggerable Delays
Sometimes an AI agent's path might be temporarily blocked by another piece. We explore how to handle the "On Fail" execution pin of the AI movement node by implementing a retriggerable delay. This ensures the engine continuously attempts to find a valid path to the target square instead of abandoning the move and breaking the game flow.

### 3. Implementing Jump and Move Logic
Animating Knights and Castling
Pieces like the Knight and the Castling Rook need to jump over other meshes. We create a custom "Jump and Move" event using Unreal Engine Timelines. You will learn how to animate relative vertical height with float curves before executing the horizontal AI movement, ensuring pieces smoothly leap into the air and land perfectly without colliding with intermediate meshes.

### 4. Enhancing Visuals with Niagara Systems
Creating Capture and Despawn Effects
To make captures and promotions feel impactful, we dive into Unreal Engine's Niagara Particle System. You will discover how to create a custom explosion effect, adjust properties like loop duration, spawn rate, and sprite size, and trigger these effects precisely when a piece is captured or despawned during a pawn promotion.

### 5. UI Integration for Pawn Promotion
Building Interactive Widgets
When a human player's pawn reaches the end of the board, they need to choose a new piece. We construct a User Interface (UI) widget Blueprint containing selectable buttons for a Queen, Rook, Knight, and Bishop. You will learn how to trigger UI animations, cast player clicks back to the game state, and seamlessly swap the physical pawn mesh with the chosen upgraded piece.

### 6. Final Testing and Project Conclusion
Validating Special Moves and Win States
In our final step, we rigorously test the game using custom FEN strings tailored to trigger specific scenarios. We successfully validate player vs player En Passants, castling rights, promotions, and AI vs AI Checkmates. Congratulations on completing the Chess-Party project! You now possess a highly sophisticated, fully functional 3D chess engine in Unreal Engine 5.

projects.title: 09 - Darts-Physics
projects.summary: Apply your UE5 skills to a brand-new challenge. Explore physics-based throwing mechanics using raycasting and physics handles to pick up and launch darts.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Welcome to the ninth lecture! Now that we have fully completed the 3D chess project, we are transitioning to a brand-new interactive system: darts. This lesson focuses exclusively on physics-based throwing mechanics. You will learn how to enable continuous collision detection, program a raycast system to pick up objects, and utilize physics handles to accurately throw and stick a dart into a cabinet.

### 1. Scene Overview and Object Collisions
Preparing the Dart and Dartboard
We start by reviewing the interactive dart meshes inside the viewport. To achieve highly precise hits—crucial for calculating dart scores later—we configure the dart's collision settings. You will learn how to enable Continuous Collision Detection (CCD) alongside physics simulation, ensuring the dart registers precise impact points without phasing through the dartboard mesh at high speeds.

### 2. Setting Up Enhanced Inputs
Mapping Keyboard and Mouse Actions
Before we can interact with the darts, we need to map player inputs. We dive into Unreal Engine's Enhanced Input System, configuring "Grab" and "Throw" input actions. You will see how to link the Left and Right Mouse buttons to these actions using an Input Mapping Context and how to assign this context directly to the player controller.

### 3. Programming the Grab Logic
Using Raytracing to Pick Up Objects
With inputs mapped, we script the grab functionality. We write a custom Raycast (Line Trace) function originating from the First Person Camera's Forward Vector. You will learn how to mathematically multiply this forward vector by a float value to define a specific "Grab Range" (e.g., 200 units), allowing the player to detect and target dart actors dynamically in the 3D world.

### 4. Mastering the Physics Handle
Moving Objects in 3D Space
Once the raycast successfully detects a dart, we need to pick it up. We utilize Unreal Engine's Physics Handle component to grab the dart at its exact transform location. To keep the dart attached to the player's screen, we hook the Physics Handle into the Event Tick, continuously updating the dart's target location and rotation to perfectly match the player's camera Billboard.

### 5. Throwing the Dart
Adding Physics Impulses
Next, we build the "Throw" logic. Upon clicking the throw input, the script releases the dart from the Physics Handle, re-enables its physics collision and gravity, and applies a massive linear impulse relative to the camera's forward vector. You will learn how to configure linear damping so the dart travels swiftly and realistically toward the target rather than floating aimlessly.

### 6. Sticking the Dart to the Board
Freezing Physics on Impact
The final step is ensuring the dart behaves like a real dart and sticks to the board upon impact. We script an "On Component Hit" event specifically checking for collisions with the Dart Cabinet class. If a valid hit occurs, we freeze the dart by setting its linear and angular damping to absurdly high values, stopping its movement instantly while retaining its exact impact coordinates.

projects.title: 10 - Darts-Projectile
projects.summary: Master the art of game dev illusions. Replace unpredictable physics with controlled projectiles and dummy meshes to guarantee perfect dart hits every time.
projects.content:
### Introduction
Welcome to the tenth and final lecture of the Applied Software Techniques course! Building on the previous lesson's physics-based darts, today we explore an alternative, highly reliable approach: Projectile-based movement. You will learn the crucial game development concept of "Fake it 'till you make it," swapping out unpredictable physics for controlled projectiles and dummy actors to guarantee perfect dartboard collisions every time.

### 1. The Flaws of Physics-Based Systems
Understanding the Need to "Fake It"
We begin by reviewing the physics dart system from the last lecture. While realistic, relying purely on the physics engine often causes unpredictable behaviors, such as darts hitting the board at awkward angles or bouncing off incorrectly. We discuss why game developers frequently "fake" complex interactions to maintain absolute control over the game's mechanics and the player's experience.

### 2. Designing the "Fake" Grab Logic
Swapping Real Darts for Dummies
Instead of picking up a physical dart with a Physics Handle, we script a new grab sequence. You will learn how to make the targeted dart instantly invisible upon selection, and simultaneously activate a "Dart Dummy" static mesh permanently attached to the player's First Person Camera. This creates the perfect optical illusion that the player is holding the dart, without any physics jitter.

### 3. Programming the Projectile Throw
Spawning Actors with Velocity
When the player clicks to throw, we do not add a physics impulse. Instead, we hide the camera dummy and dynamically spawn a new "Dart Projectile" Blueprint exactly where the camera is facing. We explore the Projectile Movement Component, setting initial speeds, max speeds, and disabling gravity so the dart flies in a perfectly straight, predictable line toward the target.

### 4. Managing Projectile Collisions
Switching States on Impact
A projectile does not use physics to fly, but it still needs to collide. We configure the projectile's collider to trigger an "On Component Begin Overlap" event when it hits the Dart Cabinet. Once triggered, the script instantly stops the projectile's movement component, switches its collision profile to "Physics Actor," and locks its linear and angular damping so it sticks perfectly into the board.

### 5. Creating the Dart Dummy Replacements
Replacing Actors in the Viewport
Because our new logic requires specific projectile actors rather than physics actors, we must update our 3D environment. You will learn a valuable Unreal Engine editor trick: using the "Replace Selected Actors With" function. This allows you to quickly swap out all the old physics darts scattered around the room with our new Projectile Dummy Blueprints in just a few clicks.

### 6. Adding Polish with Throw Animations
Triggering Skeletal Mesh Montages
To complete the illusion, we add a throwing animation. We dive briefly into the Animation Blueprint and Skeletal Mesh sockets, attaching the dart to the character's hand bone. We then script the throw event to play a custom animation montage, adding a calculated delay before the projectile spawns, ensuring the dart physically leaves the hand at the exact apex of the throwing animation.
